content.title: About
content.content: Flavored applesauce (3979) is a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected apples and enhanced with natural flavorings. It has a smooth, uniform texture, a sweet‑tart taste, and the characteristic aroma of the chosen flavor (e.g., vanilla, cinnamon, or strawberry).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Applesauce retains most of the vitamins and minerals found in fresh apples.
Natural flavorings provide variety without artificial colors.
The product is often used in baby foods because of its soft texture and easy digestibility.
Applesauce can serve as a base for sauces, desserts, and baked goods.
Sugar content is usually lower than in many ready‑made fruit desserts.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids in fluid balance and muscle function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Applesauce contains virtually no fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in apples help combat free radicals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although less sweet than many desserts, people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Apple allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to apples or added flavorings.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain versions may contain preservatives; check the label if this is a concern.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Applesauce can be enjoyed on its own, mixed into oatmeal, yogurt, smoothies, used in baking, as a pancake topping, or in baby meals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened product in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep it sealed in the refrigerator and consume within 5–7 days. Discard if you notice off‑flavors, fermentation, or color changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole wheat bread is made from whole grain wheat, retaining the bran and germ. It can be baked at home using a traditional recipe or purchased from a bakery. The loaf has a dense crumb, a slightly nutty flavor, and the aroma of fresh baking.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole wheat bread contains all parts of the grain, making it more nutritious than white bread.
Traditional home recipes often use a sourdough starter, which enhances flavor and improves nutrient bioavailability.
In many countries, whole grain bread is a staple of the Mediterranean diet, known for heart‑healthy benefits.
Bakeries frequently bake in stone ovens, giving the crust a crisp texture and distinctive aroma.
The high fiber content helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and maintains a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3, and B6 are involved in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Magnesium, iron, and zinc in whole wheat bread are important for muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white bread, whole wheat causes a slower rise in blood glucose.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Plant antioxidants and healthy fats help lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to gluten found in wheat.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Certain commercial loaves can be high in salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium options.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although healthier, whole wheat bread still provides calories; moderation is key for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the bread fresh, toasted, as a base for sandwiches, croutons, or in dishes like pita and focaccia. It pairs well with avocado, low‑fat cheese, vegetables, and lean proteins.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the loaf in a paper bag or bread box at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag for up to 2 months. Thaw and warm in the oven before serving to restore a crisp crust.

content.title: About
content.content: Granola is a mixture of rolled oats, nuts, seeds, and dried fruit baked until crisp. It is often sweetened with honey or maple syrup. Granola can be enjoyed as a standalone breakfast, added to yogurt, smoothie bowls, or used in baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Granola originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a high‑energy breakfast for athletes.
There are countless variations: nut‑free, gluten‑free, vegan, protein‑enriched, and more.
Oats, the main ingredient, are rich in beta‑glucan, which supports heart health.
Dried fruits can be dehydrated without added sugar, preserving most of their vitamins.
Granola is frequently used as a crunchy topping for ice cream and desserts.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Oats and seeds provide soluble and insoluble fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Nuts and seeds supply monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Oats deliver B1, B2, and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Supports blood sugar balance
items.content: Beta‑glucan slows carbohydrate absorption, helping to stabilize glucose levels.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Pumpkin and sunflower seeds are rich in vitamin E and selenium, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Nut and seed allergies
items.content: Granola often contains nuts, which can trigger severe allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Because of nuts and sweeteners, granola can be very calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Some commercial granolas contain added sugars, which may be undesirable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of fiber can cause bloating in those with sensitive gastrointestinal tracts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Granola can be eaten dry as a quick snack, poured over milk or plant‑based milk, mixed into yogurt, added to smoothie bowls, or incorporated into baked goods. For a softer texture, it is sometimes soaked in milk for a few minutes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store granola in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator to prevent the nuts from going rancid.

cheese-steak-sandwich-or-sub-on-wheat.title: Cheese steak sandwich or sub on wheat

content.title: About
content.content: A cheese steak sandwich or sub on wheat consists of thinly sliced beef steak, sautéed with onions and bell peppers, topped with melted cheese, and served in a soft wheat roll. It is a classic American street food originating from Philadelphia.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish appeared in the early 1900s in Philadelphia and quickly became a staple of street vendors.
Traditional cheese is American cheese, though cheddar or provolone are also common.
The term “sub” is used in the Northeastern United States for long roll sandwiches.
A wheat roll gives a softer texture compared with the classic Italian roll.
Variations may include mushrooms, bacon, or a drizzle of hoisin sauce.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Beef steak provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The sandwich supplies niacin, B6 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese adds calcium important for bone health.

items.title: Vegetable fiber
items.content: Onions and peppers provide dietary fiber and antioxidants.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Cheese and beef can raise cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt in the meat and cheese may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy should choose a dairy‑free cheese alternative.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The sandwich is relatively high in calories; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is typically served hot, cut in half. It can be dressed with mustard, mayo, or a spicy sauce. It pairs well with French fries or a coleslaw salad.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours, wrapped in foil or plastic. Reheat in an oven or grill to keep the roll crisp.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken dinner, NFS is a ready‑to‑heat frozen meal that includes chicken breast, vegetables, and a sauce. It provides a nutritious and convenient option that can be microwaved in 3–4 minutes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The meal was developed by NFS specifically for quick office and on‑the‑go meals.
The chicken undergoes double thermal processing to ensure flavor and safety.
Vegetables such as carrots, peas, and corn are flash‑frozen right after harvest.
Packaging is made from recyclable, food‑safe plastic.
The product has a shelf life of 12 months when stored at –18 °C.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The use of lean chicken makes the meal suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6 and niacin, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron and zinc, important for immune health and blood formation.

items.title: Convenient and time‑saving
items.content: Quick heating saves preparation time while preserving nutritional value.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to poultry may experience reactions when consuming this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The sauce may contain added salt; people monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Proper heating required
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave cold spots that promote bacterial growth.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Some versions contain MSG, which can cause sensitivity in certain individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Microwave the meal for 3–4 minutes, then stir to ensure even heating. Optionally garnish with fresh herbs or a squeeze of lemon for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen meal at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, consume within 2 hours and do not leave at room temperature for more than 30 minutes.

chicken-or-turkey-chow-mein-or-chop-suey.title: Chicken or Turkey Chow Mein (No Noodles)

content.title: About
content.content: A dish made from chicken or turkey meat, cooked in an Asian style with vegetables and sauce, but without noodles. The combination of tender meat, crisp vegetables, and savory soy sauce makes it a nutritious, low‑carb alternative to traditional chow mein.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional chow mein is usually prepared with egg noodles, but low‑carb versions replace the noodles with vegetables or omit them entirely.
Turkey contains less fat than chicken and is rich in selenium, which supports immune function.
The dish is often finished with sesame oil and fresh cilantro to boost aroma.
Soy sauce provides the primary umami flavor in many Asian recipes.
Skipping the noodles makes the meal suitable for keto and other low‑carb diets.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken and turkey are excellent sources of complete protein needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low carbohydrate content
items.content: The absence of noodles dramatically reduces carbs, which helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Poultry provides niacin, vitamin B6, and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish supplies iron, zinc, and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Antioxidant vegetables
items.content: Common additions like broccoli, bell pepper, and carrots are rich in vitamin C and carotenoids.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or turkey.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce can be high in salt; people with hypertension should choose low‑sodium versions.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: Undercooked meat may harbor salmonella or campylobacter; ensure thorough cooking.

items.title: Histamine intolerance
items.content: Soy sauce can trigger symptoms in those sensitive to histamine.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauté bite‑size pieces of chicken or turkey until golden, add sliced vegetables (broccoli, carrots, bell pepper), then stir‑in soy sauce, ginger, and garlic. Cook 5‑7 minutes until vegetables are tender‑crisp. Garnish with toasted sesame seeds and fresh cilantro if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer keeping, freeze it (cooled first) in a zip‑lock bag for up to 2 months.

corned-beef-potatoes-and-vegetables-incl.title: Corned Beef with Potatoes and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: Corned beef is boiled beef that has been cured in a brine solution with spices. It is served with boiled potatoes and vegetables such as carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy greens. The dish contains no sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “corned beef” comes from the English word “corn,” referring to the large salt crystals used in the curing process.
Traditionally, corned beef was popular in Ireland among the working class.
Potatoes and carrots are often boiled together with the beef, allowing them to absorb the meat’s flavor.
Broccoli and leafy greens are added at the end of cooking to keep their bright color and crisp texture.
The dish is frequently presented as a “platter” – sliced beef, potatoes, and vegetables arranged side by side.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Corned beef provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat is a good source of heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies vitamin B12, B6, and niacin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Fiber and antioxidants from vegetables
items.content: Carrots, broccoli, and leafy greens add dietary fiber, vitamin C, vitamin K, and phytochemicals.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes and broccoli are rich in potassium, helping regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Because the beef is cured in brine, the dish can be high in salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Red meat contains saturated fat; individuals with elevated cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rare, but some people may have an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Potential nitrites
items.content: Traditional curing may involve nitrites, which are considered undesirable in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, slicing the beef into strips, cutting potatoes into wedges or cubes, and chopping the vegetables into bite‑size pieces. A sprinkle of fresh herbs or a dash of lemon juice can brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Fajita is a Mexican dish that typically features thin strips of vegetables (bell pepper, onion, mushrooms) and sometimes meat, quickly sautéed over high heat. Vegetarian fajitas are made without meat, offering a crunchy texture and bright flavor, while spices such as paprika, cumin, and chili give the dish its characteristic aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The word “fajita” comes from the Spanish “faja,” meaning “strip” or “belt.”
Traditionally fajitas are cooked on a flat iron grill (plancha), which allows rapid searing of the vegetables.
Fajitas became popular in the United States in the 1970s thanks to fast‑casual restaurant chains.
Vegetable fajitas are often served with tortillas, guacamole, sour cream, and salsa.
Variations may include pineapple, zucchini, or sweet potato.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Bell peppers and onions provide vitamin C, vitamin A, and folate, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The vegetables in fajitas are low‑calorie, making the dish suitable for weight management.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Paprika and onions contain quercetin and carotenoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: When cooked with minimal oil, fajitas remain a low‑saturated‑fat meal.

items.title: Vegetable allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to peppers or onions, experiencing skin reactions or breathing difficulties.

items.title: Spicy heat
items.content: Excessive chili can irritate the stomach and esophagus in sensitive people.

items.title: Cooking contaminants
items.content: Overheating oil can produce harmful compounds; use moderate heat and fresh oil.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the vegetables into strips, heat a grill pan, add a small amount of oil and spices. Sauté for 5‑7 minutes, stirring constantly, until vegetables are tender yet crisp. Serve with warm tortillas, guacamole, salsa, and a squeeze of lime.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh vegetables in the refrigerator in an airtight container for 3‑5 days. Cooked fajita is best eaten within 24 hours; leftover portions should be kept in a sealed container in the fridge.

green-peas-frozen-cooked-with-butter-or-.title: Green peas, frozen, cooked with butter

content.title: About
content.content: Green peas are young pea pods harvested before the seeds fully mature. The frozen version retains most nutrients, and cooking with butter or margarine gives the dish a smooth, rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frozen peas are popular for quick preparation and long shelf life.
Peas belong to the legume family and are a good source of plant protein.
Freezing preserves B‑vitamins, vitamin C, and carotenoids.
Peas are traditionally used in purees, soups, and side dishes worldwide.
Pea varieties can be green or yellow depending on the cultivar.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked peas provides about 8 g of protein, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Thiamine, folate, and vitamin B6 are involved in energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Antioxidant content
items.content: Carotenoids and vitamin C protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to peas.

items.title: Sodium content in prepared dishes
items.content: If salt is added during cooking, total sodium intake should be monitored.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause bloating in sensitive people; introduce them gradually.

items.title: Caloric increase from butter
items.content: Cooking with butter or margarine adds extra calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Peas can be served as a side dish, added to soups, stews, salads, or made into a puree. Cooking with a modest amount of butter or margarine enhances flavor and improves absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen peas in the freezer at –18 °C. After thawing, use within 2–3 days and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator.

hot-chocolate-cocoa-reduced-sugar-made-w.title: Hot chocolate / cocoa, reduced sugar, made with non-dairy milk

content.title: About
content.content: Hot chocolate / cocoa with reduced sugar is made from cocoa powder, sweetened with sugar substitutes, and non‑dairy milk (soy, almond, oat, etc.). The drink delivers a rich chocolate flavor while containing far less sugar than traditional versions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cocoa powder is rich in flavonoids, which have antioxidant properties.
Lower sugar content makes the drink more suitable for people monitoring blood glucose levels.
Non‑dairy milk adds a subtle nutty note and makes the beverage vegan‑friendly.
Traditional hot chocolate originated in Mexico in the 15th century, where it was prepared from cacao beans, water, and spices.
Some sugar substitutes, like stevia, can leave a slight aftertaste that not everyone likes.

items.title: Rich in flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids in cocoa support vascular health and may help lower blood pressure.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: Helps control blood glucose levels and reduces the risk of dental caries.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cocoa provides small amounts of B1, B2, and B3 vitamins, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains magnesium, iron, and zinc, important for nervous and immune system function.

items.title: Vegan‑friendly
items.content: Absence of dairy makes it safe for those avoiding animal products.

items.title: Allergy to plant milk
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to soy, almond, or oat milk.

items.title: Sensitivity to sugar substitutes
items.content: Certain substitutes (e.g., sorbitol) can cause gastrointestinal discomfort in large amounts.

items.title: Caffeine-like compounds
items.content: Cocoa contains theobromine, which may affect sleep if consumed late in the evening.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the drink to 70‑80 °C, stirring to prevent a skin from forming. Serve in a mug; optionally add cinnamon, vanilla, or a dollop of plant‑based whipped topping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry ingredients (cocoa powder, sweetener) in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Opened non‑dairy milk should be kept in the refrigerator and used within 5‑7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Salmon sushi roll is a traditional Japanese dish consisting of vinegared rice, nori seaweed, and fresh salmon fillet. The roll is typically served with soy sauce, wasabi, and pickled ginger. Salmon gives the roll a delicate flavor, a vivid pink color, and valuable omega‑3 fatty acids.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sushi originated in Southeast Asia as a method of preserving fish in rice.
Salmon in sushi is often used raw, but it can also be lightly seared or marinated.
In Japan it is customary to eat sushi with chopsticks, though many people prefer using their hands for rolls.
Nori sheets are rich in iodine and B‑vitamins.
There are over 200 types of sushi rolls, yet the classic salmon roll remains one of the most popular worldwide.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Salmon provides EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: The roll delivers complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Salmon and rice contain B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Selenium, phosphorus and potassium in the roll contribute to normal bodily functions.

items.title: Moderate calorie count
items.content: One roll (about 6–8 pieces) provides roughly 200–250 kcal, fitting well into a balanced diet.

items.title: Food‑borne infection risk
items.content: Raw salmon may contain parasites and bacteria; only use fish that has been inspected for safety.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to seafood should avoid this roll.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce and pickled ginger add salt, so people with hypertension should limit usage.

items.title: Mercury content
items.content: While salmon generally has low mercury levels, pregnant women and children should limit raw fish intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The roll is usually eaten with chopsticks, dipped in soy sauce. Add a dab of wasabi for heat and ginger for palate cleansing. It can also be cut into smaller bite‑size pieces if preferred.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared roll refrigerated at 0–4 °C and consume within 24 hours. For longer storage, freezing is possible, though the rice texture may change.
